description:
PWC coach-narrates-own-move surface (2026-05-26). Fires when the central layer is called with coach_move_context set (caption_pipeline.inject_coach_move_facts stamps coach_move_is_active=True). Produces the multi-field CoachExtras shape that smart_coaching.generate_smart_coach_explanation produces today via an LLM call — but deterministically, from caption_facts. See memory/feedback_one_source_of_truth.

Unlike R01-R15 (single-caption rules), R17 variants are OBJECTS with explanation / plan / teaching_point / hint_for_user fields. Rendered by populate_coach_extras_from_r17 in caption_pipeline.py — NOT through the generic render_rule path. Variant selection still uses select_variant predicates against caption_facts.

fact_glossary.captured_piece_type: When move was a capture: piece-type taken (e.g. 'pawn', 'knight')
fact_glossary.coach_move_is_active: Gate flag — true when coach_move_context was supplied to build_move_teaching_decision
fact_glossary.coach_target_was_undefended: True iff move was a capture AND captured square had no defenders BEFORE the move (free piece)
fact_glossary.coach_attack_targets: List of {piece, square, defender_count, attacker_count} for opp non-king pieces the moved piece now attacks
fact_glossary.coach_attack_first_target_piece: Computed by renderer: piece-name of the first entry in coach_attack_targets when any (e.g. 'knight')
fact_glossary.coach_attack_first_target_square: Computed by renderer: square of the first attack target (e.g. 'c6')
fact_glossary.coach_attack_first_target_undefended: Computed by renderer: true iff first attack target has defender_count==0
fact_glossary.coach_v2_sub_attacks_undefended: v2 sub_scores.attacks_undefended pass-through (>0 means coach now threatens undefended)
fact_glossary.coach_v2_sub_capture_punishment: v2 sub_scores.capture_punishment pass-through (>0 means coach captured undefended)
fact_glossary.coach_v2_sub_checks: v2 sub_scores.checks pass-through (>0 means coach has check available)

coach_capture_free.plan: Before every move, check: is anything I own undefended?
coach_capture_free.teaching_point: Count attackers vs defenders on every piece before you move.
coach_capture_free.hint_for_user: Scan the board: which of your pieces has no defender right now?

coach_capture_trade.plan: When trading, ask: does this exchange help my position or hurt it?
coach_capture_trade.teaching_point: Don't trade for the sake of trading — trade when it improves your structure or activity.
coach_capture_trade.hint_for_user: Was this trade good for me or for the coach? Count the squares each side now controls.

coach_creates_fork.explanation: {played_san} — this piece is now attacking two of your pieces at once.
coach_creates_fork.plan: You can only save one. Pick the more valuable target — accept losing the other or find a counter-threat.
coach_creates_fork.teaching_point: Double attacks (forks) win material because the opponent can't save everything in one move.
coach_creates_fork.hint_for_user: Count what this piece is attacking. Which target is more valuable, and can you find a tempo move that saves both?

coach_gives_check.plan: Forced moves first: address the check before considering anything else.
coach_gives_check.teaching_point: Checks are the most forcing move in chess. Always answer a check before your own plans.
coach_gives_check.hint_for_user: What are your three ways out of check: block, capture the checker, or move the king?

coach_threatens_hanging.explanation: {played_san} — one of your pieces is now undefended. Can you find which one?
coach_threatens_hanging.plan: After every opponent move, ask: did anything change? Is something now attacked or undefended?
coach_threatens_hanging.teaching_point: The single biggest habit improving players develop: pause after each opponent move and re-scan the board.
coach_threatens_hanging.hint_for_user: Look at every piece you own — is there one with attackers but no defenders?

coach_threat_undefended.explanation: {played_san} — attacks your {coach_attack_first_target_piece} on {coach_attack_first_target_square}, and it has no defender.
coach_threat_undefended.plan: Before you play, ask: what is my opponent threatening?
coach_threat_undefended.teaching_point: The #1 habit of improving players: check what changed after the opponent's move.
coach_threat_undefended.hint_for_user: Your {coach_attack_first_target_piece} on {coach_attack_first_target_square} is attacked and undefended — can you defend it, move it, or counter-attack?

coach_threat_specific.plan: When a piece is attacked, the three responses are: defend, move, or counter-threat.
coach_threat_specific.teaching_point: Always identify what each opponent move attacks before choosing your reply.
coach_threat_specific.hint_for_user: How will you handle the threat on {coach_attack_first_target_square}?

coach_threat_general.explanation: {played_san} — what changed on the board for you?
coach_threat_general.plan: Always ask: what does my opponent's move do? Attacks, threats, or just positioning?
coach_threat_general.teaching_point: Most blunders happen because a player didn't notice what the opponent's last move actually did.
coach_threat_general.hint_for_user: Re-scan: is anything new attacked, defended, or pinned after my move?

coach_castles_kingside.explanation: O-O — castling kingside to get my king safe.
coach_castles_kingside.plan: Castle early too — a safe king lets you play more aggressively in the middlegame.
coach_castles_kingside.teaching_point: Castling does two things at once: it tucks your king behind pawns AND activates your rook.
coach_castles_kingside.hint_for_user: Have you castled yet? If not, plan it within the next few moves.

coach_castles_queenside.plan: Queenside castles trade a faster king-shelter for an immediately active rook on the d-file.
coach_castles_queenside.teaching_point: Queenside castling is sharper — the king is slightly more exposed but the rook hits the center faster.
coach_castles_queenside.hint_for_user: Where's your king safer this game — kingside or queenside?

coach_opening_develop_knight.explanation: {played_san} — developing the knight toward the center.
coach_opening_develop_knight.plan: Knights belong on c3/f3/c6/f6 in most openings. They control more squares from there than from the edge.
coach_opening_develop_knight.teaching_point: Develop knights before bishops — knights need more moves to reach active squares.
coach_opening_develop_knight.hint_for_user: Are your knights developed yet, or still on the back rank?

coach_opening_develop_bishop.explanation: {played_san} — developing the bishop to an active diagonal.
coach_opening_develop_bishop.plan: Bishops need open diagonals. Place them where they see the whole board, not blocked by their own pawns.
coach_opening_develop_bishop.teaching_point: Develop pieces toward the center, then castle, then connect rooks.
coach_opening_develop_bishop.hint_for_user: Do your bishops have open diagonals, or are they stuck behind their own pawns?

coach_opening_central_pawn.explanation: {played_san} — controlling the center with a pawn.
coach_opening_central_pawn.plan: Central pawns claim space and open lines for your pieces to develop into.
coach_opening_central_pawn.teaching_point: Control the center first, then develop pieces around your pawn structure.
coach_opening_central_pawn.hint_for_user: Are you contesting the center, or letting the coach control it?

coach_opening_generic.plan: Develop pieces, control the center, castle early — in that order.
coach_opening_generic.teaching_point: The opening is about getting pieces active and the king safe, not about creating threats.
coach_opening_generic.hint_for_user: What's your slowest piece right now? Develop it next.

coach_quiet_repositioning.plan: Strong players make small improvements between bigger plans — every move should make some piece better.
coach_quiet_repositioning.teaching_point: Not every move needs to be a tactical strike — quiet positioning compounds into a winning position.
coach_quiet_repositioning.hint_for_user: Look at your worst piece. What's the best square it could reach in two moves?
